# ONS Analysis Standards and Pipelines hub, quality assurance of code for analysis and research (the Duck Book)

**Source:** Analysis Standards and Pipelines hub, Office for National Statistics, for the UK Government Analysis Function. *Quality assurance of code for analysis and research* ("the Duck Book"), web book, version 2026.1, repository commit fa39f20 (2026-06-09); suggested citation "UK Government Analytical Community. (2020)". No individual authors named. Open Government Licence v3.0. Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0; this reference paraphrases and quotes the source.
**Scope:** open
**Structure:** a root page and 18 chapters: glossary, managers' guide, a checklists stub, principles, then practice chapters (modular and readable code, project structure, code and project documentation, version control, configuration, data, peer review, testing, automation), learning resources, tools, and a work-in-progress chapter on generative AI. Cited as `(book/{file}.md, "Section heading")`.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The book is Government Analysis Function guidance that "describes software engineering good practices that are tailored to those working with data using code" [V], written to help analysts quality assure their code and make their analyses reproducible; software built this way is called a reproducible analytical pipeline (RAP) (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book"). It rests on three founding principles, each supported by the one before: reproducible, auditable, assured. Reproducibility comes first, because "Reproducibility is the only thing that you can guarantee in your analysis." [V] (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"). Assurance is proportionate, "the right quality assurance procedures for the right analysis" [V] (book/principles.md, "Assured"), following the Aqua book.

The frame behind the practice chapters is that "when we write code for analysis, we are developing software" [V] (book/readable_code.md, "Software ideas for analysts"), so analysts should adopt software engineering practice at least in part. A manager need not read the code to trust it, provided the team has taken an appropriate approach and applies proportionate assurance; where code assurance falls short of the agreed target, the manager adds assurance of the outputs, such as dual running (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). A final chapter, marked a work in progress, extends the guidance to LLM coding assistants: it explains why they produce plausible but inaccurate code, sets three golden rules (review LLM code yourself before using or submitting it, you alone are responsible for it, never enter sensitive information into a chatbot), and argues for directing the model rather than picking up after it (book/generative_ai.md).

## Purpose, audience and status

The book serves people who write code to automate their work, build statistical or data-engineering pipelines, develop models or data science techniques, or want an introduction to software engineering for analysis; it is language agnostic, gives examples in Python and R, and does not aim to be a full learning resource (book/intro.md, "How to get the most out of the book"). It is a living document versioned by calendar year (book/intro.md; book/project_documentation.md, "Versioning").

The book flags its own unfinished parts: draft banners on the glossary and the managers' guide (which asks for case studies on deciding the level of assurance), a checklists page saying the checklists have been removed while being updated though other chapters still point to them, a TDD section "framed more like training" [V], a `{todo}` diagram, and a work-in-progress note on the generative AI chapter (book/glossary.md; book/managers_guide.md; book/checklists.md; book/testing_code.md, "Write tests before writing logic"; book/data.md, "Version control data"; book/generative_ai.md).

## Principles of good analysis

Reproducible analysis guarantees "that we have done what we are claiming to have done, and that others can easily replicate our work" [V]; auditable analysis records why it was chosen and who is responsible for each part; assured analysis improves average quality and communicates it to users (book/principles.md, "Principles"). Reproducibility relies on documentation that shows how methodology and implementation map to each other, and further assurances such as peer review and testing are called secondary to it (book/principles.md, "Reproducible"). Auditable analysis can answer who made each decision, when, and on what evidence (book/principles.md, "Auditable").

Assurance is proportionate: analysis that decisions rest on is held to high standards, analysts are not overburdened where it does not, "Assurance is best demonstrated through peer review." [V], dual running should be considered for high-risk analysis, and guarantees of assurance should be published with the report (book/principles.md, "Assured"). The book sets RAP against manual and semi-manual production with proprietary tools and office software, which it calls time-consuming and error-prone because inputs and outputs connect only through manual intervention (book/principles.md, "Reproducible analytical pipelines").

## Managing analytical code development

A manager "should not need an in-depth understanding of the analysis code to trust that it is working correctly" [V], but should be confident the team took an appropriate approach and applies proportionate assurance; managers agree with the team which practices each piece of analysis needs, ideally before work starts, and weigh team skills alongside risk, growing them one step at a time (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk"). Skipping good practice creates technical debt, which may be necessary for short deadlines but needs time set aside; where code assurance misses the target, "for example where there is limited time or skill" [V], managers supplement it with in-depth assurance of outputs such as dual running and consistency checks (book/managers_guide.md, "Apply quality assurance proportional to risk").

The guide then gives question sets. For design: why this approach (users consulted, more than one developer, open-source tools), how input data is stored and versioned, and how code changes and their reasons are tracked (book/managers_guide.md, "Design quality analysis"). For development: code structure, configuration, documentation, dependencies, assumptions (which "You must communicate these to users when releasing results from the analysis." [V]), peer review of each change, testing with realistic and edge-case data and a test for each identified error, failure behaviour and logging, comparison with previous results, and continued improvement (book/managers_guide.md, "Quality assure throughout development").

## Writing code

Modular code underpins the other practices: repeated code becomes functions with no hidden side-effects, related functions become modules and packages, and classes hide state and distribute responsibility, with encapsulation preferred to inheritance for reuse (book/modular_code.md). Scripts run end to end are preferred to notebooks for producing outputs, since "Output generation should instead be trusted to scripts, where human decisions do not alter the order that code is run." [V] (book/modular_code.md, "Think carefully about whether notebooks are a suitable way to organise your code").

Readable code starts with informative names and a consistent style, but style compliance is not the goal, and style checks should be automated (book/readable_code.md). The section "Software ideas for analysts" condenses engineering principles: keep it simple and capture requirements before coding, don't repeat yourself (a third uncorrected copy leaves "a bug sleeping in the code waiting to be triggered" [V]), be explicit, give each function or class one responsibility, and keep code open to extension but closed to modification (book/readable_code.md, "Software ideas for analysts").

## Structure and documentation

Analysis is organised as a directed acyclic graph from raw inputs to outputs, raw data is preserved read-only, scripts run end to end in a clean environment, and outputs are disposable: worry about deleting them signals a lack of confidence in reproducing them (book/project_structure.md). Comments explain why rather than what, because "the only point of 'truth' is the code that is executed" [V]; toggling behaviour by commenting code in and out is highly discouraged (book/code_documentation.md, "Comments").

Docstrings document functions close to the code, and "The documentation should be a specification of what the code is expected to do." [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "Docstrings"). AI assistants can save time writing documentation, but the output must be checked, requirements kept bounded, and "Do not expect a coding assistant to document your entire application correctly with minimal intervention." [V] (book/code_documentation.md, "AI coding assistants"). Project documentation covers README, contributing guidance, user desk instructions that state what assurance "has been carried out and what further quality assurance of outputs is required" [V], dependencies, versioning, changelogs, licences and open-sourcing (book/project_documentation.md).

## Version control, configuration and data

Version control keeps an audit trail of what changed, when, why and by whom; a remote repository "maintains a single source of truth" [V]; commits are small and single-purpose; branching is proportional to the work; and merges to `main` can be blocked "without an approved Pull Request to enforce peer review" [V] (book/version_control.md). Credentials, real configuration and sensitive data never enter the repository; access control is no substitute for that discipline, and a leaked secret requires rewriting history, not just deleting the file (book/version_control.md, "Avoid committing sensitive information to Git repositories"; "Handle data breaches via Git").

Configuration that changes between runs lives in separate files passed as arguments, so the configuration that produced each output is on record, and secrets live in environment variables (book/configuration.md). Data is stored in open formats, never in spreadsheets for storage or production, documented, and versioned, since "it is your responsibility to ensure you identify the exact data that you have used" [V] (book/data.md, "Spreadsheets"; "Version control data").

## Peer review

Peer review is "a quality assurance activity where a developer, other than the code's author, views and tests the usage of a piece of code" [V]; it is proportionate to complexity and business risk, with external review recommended for novel, complex or business-critical analysis (book/peer_review.md, "Peer review"). Reviewers ask whether they understand the code, whether testing is proportionate to the risk, how easily the code can change, and whether they can reproduce the claimed outputs, rather than dwelling on layout and style (book/peer_review.md, "Focus reviews on code quality").

Feedback is documented with the code version and acted on or justified before the analysis is used (book/peer_review.md, "Document review feedback and outcomes"). Pair programming is recommended as the most timely review method; separate review works best on small, frequent changes, and "If a project is only reviewed when all of the code has been written, this significantly reduces the benefit of review." [V] (book/peer_review.md, "Give timely feedback"; "Review separately when necessary").

## Testing

"You cannot confirm your code works correctly if you don’t carry out tests, so you cannot be confident that your analysis is fit for purpose without them." [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Testing code"). Testing is risk-based; tests are reproducible, repeatable and deterministic, so "the only reason for a test to fail should be that the code being tested is incorrect" [V]; all tests run on every change; outcomes are recorded with the code version (book/testing_code.md, "Write repeatable tests"; "Run all tests against each change to your code"; "Record the outcomes of your tests").

Test data is minimal, fake and readable, and "You must not copy the output from running your code to create your expected test outcomes." [V] (book/testing_code.md, "Minimise your test data"). Unit, integration and end-to-end tests are layered; external systems are isolated with mocks whose calls are asserted; each bug gets a test; TDD is called best practice; and skipping tests in a time crunch needs a plan to return to them (book/testing_code.md).

## Automating quality assurance

Automated test runs establish trust "by ensuring that all unit tests pass before every merge" [V] (book/continuous_integration.md, "Motivation"). Small changes are committed often, Git hooks stop failing commits, linters and formatters run automatically, and CI workflows test every push and pull request, where a failure "can block the merge" [V] (book/continuous_integration.md).

## Generative AI

LLMs are "next-word-predictor machines" [V] and black boxes; they "can and regularly do generate **plausible but inaccurate** statements" [V], which the book calls "mathematically inevitable" [V] and a feature rather than a failure, since models are trained only to produce outputs that look right (book/generative_ai.md, "Introduction - Machine learning and Large Language Models"; "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace"). Hence three golden rules: never use or submit LLM code to peer review without first reviewing it yourself; "The only person responsible for the code you generated with an LLM is you." [V]; and never enter sensitive information into a chatbot (book/generative_ai.md, "Vibe coding: Using LLMs to write code in the workplace").

The chapter weighs cited evidence [BT]: one study found AI-assisted programmers produced more pull requests and builds but no significant difference in successful builds, and another found experienced programmers took longer with AI while believing they were faster; it adds risks to on-the-job learning, wellbeing, security, the environment and ethics (book/generative_ai.md, "Don't kill my vibe - The benefits of vibe coding"; "Vibe check failed - The risks of vibe coding"). Its conclusion, after a CoPilot example in which a vague prompt returned 225 lines and a precise one 46, is that "LLM-powered chatbots are most useful when you direct them to work for you, rather than when you are picking up after them and trying to shape their outputs into something functional." [V] (book/generative_ai.md, "Conclusion - Centaurs and reverse-centaurs").

## Key Connections

- The Aqua book: source of proportionality and of most departments' assurance guidance (book/managers_guide.md; book/principles.md; book/peer_review.md).
- Wider UK government and statistical-system guidance on service design, RAP, quality, data quality and AI, cited as directive [BT].
- Published DevOps research and RAP case studies, linked as evidence that good practice raises efficiency and maintainability [BT].
- Software design principles the book teaches (single responsibility, separation of concerns, open-closed, don't repeat yourself, keep it simple) and published Git practice, cited [BT].
- Review practice: a structured feedback model, published guidance on pair programming, and an open peer review of a public-health R package as a case study [BT].
- Generative AI studies cited for findings on hallucination, productivity, learning, wellbeing and security, and a borrowed centaur and reverse-centaur framing [BT].

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Proprietary analysis software (SAS, SPSS, Stata) and its data formats do not support reproducible practice.
2. Manual and semi-manual production processes are time-consuming and error-prone.
3. Spreadsheets should not be used to store data or to produce statistics and models.
4. Notebooks are not suitable for modularising pipelines or generating outputs.
5. Switching behaviour by commenting code in and out is highly discouraged.
6. Following a style guide is not the goal of good code.
7. Encapsulation beats inheritance for reuse; Responsibility Driven Design may beat Data Driven Design for complex work.
8. Expected test outcomes must never be copied from the code's own output.
9. Reviewing only once all the code is written loses much of review's value.
10. Access control does not replace good version-control practice, and deleting a leaked file does not fix a breach.
11. LLM-generated code must not be used unreviewed, and offloading the design to the model turns the user into a reverse-centaur.
